title: Architecture
content:
Architecture The diagram is drawn in draw.io with the official AWS icons, and the editable source is docs/diagrams/architecture.drawio in the repository. The numbers on the arrows match the steps below. Everything runs in one region, ap-southeast-1 (Singapore).
Flow 1 - Receiving Carrier Events (steps 1-6) A carrier (or the replayer) sends a webhook to API Gateway. Webhooks authenticate with a shared secret header, not with Cognito. The API Lambda picks the adapter for that carrier, maps the payload to one of eight common statuses, and computes a deterministic eventId from the content. The event is put on an SQS FIFO queue with the shipment as the message group, and the carrier gets 202 Accepted right away. The Processor Lambda takes events one shipment at a time. A small state machine decides whether each one is Applied, Stale, Rejected, or Duplicate, and DynamoDB saves the new status and the history item in one transaction. The processor also appends the event to the S3 data bucket under events/dt=YYYY-MM-DD/ as JSON lines. It publishes delivered and late-delivery counts to CloudWatch, per carrier. A message that fails five times moves to a dead-letter queue, which has its own alarm. Every 15 minutes, EventBridge Scheduler starts the Replayer Lambda, which reads the next Olist orders from S3 and sends them through exactly the same path as a real carrier (S1-S2).
Flow 2 - Staff Using the Dashboard (steps 7-11) The browser loads the website from CloudFront. The web bucket is private, and only CloudFront can read it, through Origin Access Control. The user signs in with Cognito (authorization code + PKCE) and receives a token that says which group they belong to. The browser calls API Gateway with that token. The gateway rejects a missing or expired token (401), and the Lambda rejects the wrong role (403). To look up a shipment, the Lambda runs one DynamoDB query that returns the status and the whole history. For SLA reports, the Lambda runs SQL in Athena over the event lake. The table schema lives in the Glue Data Catalog. Flow 3 - Alerts (steps 12-13) A CloudWatch alarm fires when the late-delivery rate is 20% or more in 2 of 3 consecutive 15-minute windows, or when the dead-letter queue is not empty. SNS emails the on-call person, once when the problem starts and once when it is over. Deployment Pushing to main runs GitHub Actions. Tests run first, then the workflow waits for my approval, then it gets a temporary IAM role through OIDC and deploys the stack with AWS SAM / CloudFormation. No AWS access key is stored on GitHub.
Why These Services Need Choice Reason Keep events for one shipment in order, while different shipments still run in parallel SQS FIFO, message group = shipment FIFO guarantees order inside a group, and groups are processed in parallel Handle the same webhook twice safely Deterministic eventId + DynamoDB condition The second copy becomes Duplicate and writes nothing Status and history must never disagree DynamoDB transaction with a version number Both items are written together, and two writers cannot overwrite each other Pay only for what is used Lambda (arm64), DynamoDB on-demand, no VPC No servers, no NAT gateway, and arm64 costs about 20% less than x86 SLA analysis without a database server S3 + Athena + partition projection Queries scan only the days they need, with no crawler Login with two roles Cognito + the API Gateway JWT authorizer Bad tokens are stopped at the gateway before Lambda runs Host the website S3 + CloudFront with OAC HTTPS at almost no cost, and the bucket stays private Deploy without long-lived keys GitHub OIDC + approval A leaked repository secret cannot be used to deploy Well-Architected View Operational excellence: the whole stack is one SAM template. A one-command daily check reports 10 health items. Deployment is automated and needs approval. Security: Cognito login with roles, webhook secret, private buckets, CloudFront security headers, a permissions boundary on every role, API throttling, input validation, and no stored keys. Reliability: FIFO ordering, idempotent writes, transactions, partial batch failure with a DLQ, and a replayer that never skips a failed order. Performance efficiency: the median time from webhook to stored status was 17 ms (p95 40 ms) in the chaos test. A two-layer cache means 79% of report queries do not scan S3. Cost optimization: serverless on arm64, on-demand DynamoDB, a 1 GB cap per Athena query, partition projection, and 14-day log retention.

title: Architecture and Design
content:
Architecture and Design Architecture as deployed after 23 November 2026, drawn in draw.io with AWS icons. Source: docs/diagrams/architecture.drawio in the repository.
How a Run Flows flowchart LR EB[EventBridge 01:00 UTC+7] --> SF[Step Functions] SF <--> LOCK[DynamoDB lock] API[4 public job APIs] --> ING[Glue Python Shell] SF -.-> ING ING --> BR[S3 Bronze + manifest] BR --> SI[Glue Spark: Silver + Data Quality] SF -.-> SI SI --> GO[Glue Spark: Gold] SF -.-> GO GO --> ICE[S3 Gold as Iceberg tables] ICE --> CAT[Glue Data Catalog] SF --> MARK[Completion marker with snapshot ids] CAT --> AT[Athena] MARK -.-> DASH[Streamlit dashboard, local] AT --> DASH M15[EventBridge every 15 min] --> HM[Lambda health monitor] M15 --> JAN[Lambda lock janitor] HM --> CW[CloudWatch alarms] --> SNS[SNS email] JAN -.-> LOCK A run goes through five stages:
At 01:00 Vietnam time, EventBridge starts one Step Functions execution. The first thing it does is take a lock in DynamoDB, so two runs can never write at the same time. A Glue Python Shell job calls the 36 job boards (five at a time), saves each raw answer to the Bronze area of S3, and writes a manifest last. Nothing later reads a file that the manifest does not list. A Glue Spark job turns Bronze into Silver. It works out which postings are new, still open, or closed, and stops the run if the Glue Data Quality rules fail. A second Spark job builds three Gold tables and commits each one as an Apache Iceberg table. Step Functions then writes a completion marker that records the exact Iceberg snapshot of every table. Every 15 minutes, a health-monitor Lambda checks that the published data is fresh and complete, and alarms through SNS if it is not. A second Lambda, the lock janitor, frees a lock that an aborted run left behind. Why Each Service Need Service I chose Why not something else Store raw and processed data cheaply Amazon S3 One run per day does not justify a database that runs all the time Call HTTP APIs Glue Python Shell The work is small. A Spark cluster would cost more and start slower Join and reconcile thousands of rows Glue Spark + Glue Data Quality Managed Spark, with quality rules built in Run stages in order, wait, and clean up on failure Step Functions A plain cron cannot release a lock or check results between stages Make sure only one writer runs DynamoDB conditional write A lock with a timer could expire while Glue is still writing Make each day’s Gold change all-or-nothing Apache Iceberg Each table commit is atomic, and readers can pin an exact version Run SQL without a server Athena Query volume is far too low for Redshift Watch the pipeline from outside Lambda + CloudWatch + SNS The monitor still works when the pipeline itself is broken Describe all of the above Terraform Every resource and permission is reviewed in a plan before it changes Well-Architected View Operational excellence: everything is in Terraform. Six CloudWatch alarms cover failed, timed-out, and aborted runs, unhealthy data, low source coverage, and janitor errors. Runbooks describe recovery. Security: each stage has its own IAM role, the dashboard can only read, buckets are private and accept HTTPS only, and no access keys are stored. Checkov scans the Terraform code on every pull request. Reliability: the manifest is the commit point, the writer lock is released only on evidence, failed or truncated boards never close postings, and Gold changes are atomic. Performance efficiency: API calls run in parallel with a bounded queue that fits the 1 GB Python Shell. Spark runs only where data is joined. Athena reads one pinned snapshot, about 1 MiB per dashboard query. Cost optimization: the pipeline runs once a day, uses the smallest Glue workers, sets lifecycle rules on every bucket, and caps each Athena query at 10 GiB. Removing the Glue crawler cut about 44% of the Glue cost per run. Known Trade-offs The three Gold tables commit one after another, not in a single transaction. The completion marker solves this for readers: it names one consistent set of snapshot ids. The dashboard runs on my own machine. It is a viewer for the published data, not a public website.

title: OnTime Radar - Shipment SLA Service
content:
OnTime Radar - Shipment SLA Service The Problem An online shop in Vietnam usually ships through two to four carriers at once, such as GHN, GHTK, and J&T. Each carrier has its own status codes, its own tracking page, and its own webhook format. In practice this causes four problems:
Customer service opens several websites to answer one question: “where is my order?” The shop learns that a parcel is late only when the customer complains. Nobody can say which carrier delivers on time in which region, so carriers are chosen by feel. Webhooks arrive twice or out of order, so a parcel’s status can jump backwards. What I Built OnTime Radar is a serverless backend and web dashboard. It receives status events from every carrier and keeps one trusted timeline per shipment:
One status model. A small adapter per carrier maps its codes onto eight shared statuses. Correct order, no duplicates. Events for the same shipment are processed one at a time. Repeated events are ignored, and late or impossible updates are recorded without changing the status. One place to look. A single API call returns a shipment’s current status and its full history. Early warning. When the share of late deliveries stays high, CloudWatch raises an alarm and SNS sends an email with a link to the list of problem orders. SLA reports. Every event is also stored in S3, and Athena answers questions such as “on-time rate per carrier and region over the last 30 days”. A dashboard with roles. Staff sign in with Cognito. Customer-service accounts can look up orders, and managers can also see the SLA reports. The traffic is real data replayed: a scheduled Lambda replays about 98,000 historical orders from the public Olist e-commerce dataset as carrier webhooks, every 15 minutes. Order dates, delivery dates, promised dates, and regions come from the dataset. Carrier names, tracking codes, and in-transit steps are simulated.
Who Uses It User Login role What they need Customer service cskh Answer “where is my order?” in seconds Operations staff cskh Know immediately which orders are in trouble Operations manager manager Compare carriers by region with real numbers Carrier systems webhook secret Push status updates AWS Services Used API Gateway (HTTP API), AWS Lambda (.NET 10, arm64), Amazon SQS FIFO, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Athena, Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, Amazon Cognito, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon SNS, AWS IAM, and AWS SAM / CloudFormation. Deployments run from GitHub Actions through OIDC.

title: AWS for Software & Financial Services Companies Day
content:
AWS for Software & Financial Services Companies Day Event Information Date: 08 October 2026 Location: Sheraton Saigon Grand Opera Organizer: Amazon Web Services (AWS) Workshop track attended: Track B - Build & Deploy AI Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Using Vibe Coding with Kiro Event Overview The event brought together AWS specialists and technology practitioners to discuss production-ready AI agents, high-quality data products for AI, agentic cloud migration, and practical development with Kiro and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The program included three technical presentations, two parallel workshop tracks, a customer spotlight, and closing remarks.
Welcome and Opening Speaker: Hung Gia - Manager, Solutions Architecture, AWS
The opening introduced the event agenda and its focus on agentic AI, modern data foundations, cloud migration, modernization, and hands-on learning.
Session 1 - From Demo to Deployment: Solving Agentic AI’s Toughest Challenges Speaker: Dzung Ha - Solutions Architect, AWS
The session explained the gap between an AI proof of concept and a production-ready system through four pillars:
Operational Excellence: observability, cost control, scale, latency, and governance. Data and Context: data quality, retrieval, RAG, grounding, and short-term and long-term memory. Reliability: deterministic code, evaluations, continuous testing, monitoring, and recovery. Trust: identity, session isolation, policies, security boundaries, privacy, and guardrails. The session also introduced Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory, AgentCore Evaluations, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. The main lesson was that a working model alone is not enough; a production agent also requires reliable data, monitoring, evaluation, security, and governance.
What I found especially useful was the speaker’s progression from a familiar problem - many AI proofs of concept never reach production - to a structured production framework. Instead of presenting individual AWS services in isolation, the speaker connected each service to an operational question: whether the system can be observed, whether its context is trustworthy, whether its behavior can be evaluated, and whether it remains within defined boundaries. The examples around context windows, memory, RAG quality, model evaluation, and guardrails helped me see an AI agent as a complete software system rather than only a model and prompt.
I also learned an important engineering principle from this session: deterministic code should still be used for calculations, validation, and rule-based work, while the agent should be reserved for tasks that genuinely require reasoning. This approach can reduce cost and latency while making the overall system easier to test and troubleshoot.
Session 2 - Building High-Quality Data Products for AI Agents Speaker: Binh Tran - Senior Solutions Architect, AWS
This session described five characteristics of AI-ready data: trusted, contextual, traceable, governed, and operational. The main topics included:
Data product ownership, operating models, and service-level expectations. Data contracts covering schemas, quality rules, freshness, versioning, and access. Enforcing data quality close to the source with services such as AWS Glue Data Quality. Technical and business metadata, lineage, semantic layers, business glossaries, and ontologies. Fine-grained access control with IAM, AWS Lake Formation, Cedar policies, and agent identity. Interoperable access through open table formats and AWS MCP Servers. RAG, vector and graph retrieval, Text-to-SQL, and safeguards before an agent changes a live system. The key takeaway was that agents need explicit business meaning, validated data, traceability, freshness guarantees, and restricted access before they can make reliable decisions or take actions.
The presentation style in this session was valuable because the speaker used one data error and followed it through the source, pipeline, catalog, semantic layer, agent, and final action. This made the consequences of weak data quality easy to understand: an error may not cause a technical failure, but it can still lead an agent to make a confident and harmful decision. The data-contract example clarified how ownership, schema, business meaning, quality rules, freshness, versioning, and access should be defined together instead of being handled as separate concerns.
Several concepts were new or became clearer to me during this session. I learned why technical metadata alone is insufficient for an agent and how a business glossary, semantic layer, ground-truth examples, and entity relationships provide the context that people often understand implicitly. I also gained a clearer view of layered authorization: an agent needs its own identity, a limited service role, permissions delegated on behalf of a user, filtered access to data, and policy checks before calling tools or APIs. This changed my understanding of data preparation from simple cleaning and transformation into the design of a governed product that an agent can safely consume.
Session 3 - Migration at Scale with Agentic AI: AWS Transform and Beyond Speaker: Taiki Dang - Solutions Architect, Migration & Modernize | Security, AWS
The session covered the evolution from traditional migration to AI-assisted and agentic migration. It introduced AWS Transform and its integration with Kiro, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Cloud Migration Factory, and AWS Transform for VMware.
Three migration patterns were presented:
Assist: use AI on top of a proven Cloud Migration Factory execution model. Automate: use AWS Transform across the migration lifecycle with human approval gates. Orchestrate: combine AWS Transform, Kiro, and AgentCore agents for migration and coordination work. The session also discussed rehosting, replatforming, containerization, Windows and mainframe modernization, custom transformations, and customer examples from global organizations and Vietnam. The main lesson was that agents can automate migration workstreams while humans retain responsibility for important decisions and approvals.
The speaker made a complex migration topic easier to follow by first explaining the limitations of traditional, human-coordinated migration and then comparing it with AI-assisted and agentic approaches. The three patterns - Assist, Automate, and Orchestrate - gave me a practical way to understand that organizations do not need to adopt the same level of automation. The appropriate approach depends on compliance requirements, existing tools, team readiness, and the need for human approval, not only on the number of servers or applications.
I learned that agentic migration is not simply about generating scripts faster. It also involves discovery, planning, landing-zone and network preparation, worklog traceability, approval gates, execution, validation, and coordination across teams. The examples of AWS Transform as the execution engine, Kiro as the conversational interface, and AgentCore agents handling coordination tasks showed how multiple tools can share context while people continue to control high-impact decisions.
Learning from the Speakers and Session Structure One of my main reasons for attending this event was to observe how AWS specialists communicate advanced technical topics. The speakers did not begin with long lists of services. They first established a real problem, explained why existing approaches were insufficient, and then introduced architecture patterns and AWS capabilities as responses to that problem. This made each session easier to follow and gave the technical details a clear purpose.
I noticed several presentation techniques that I can apply to my own technical work:
Start with the business or operational risk before describing the technology. Organize a large topic into a small number of memorable pillars or patterns. Use one scenario throughout a session so the audience can follow cause and effect. Compare alternatives and trade-offs instead of presenting one service as the answer to every problem. Connect architecture diagrams to responsibilities, permissions, data flow, and failure handling. Finish with concrete takeaways so the audience understands what should change in practice. The three sessions also connected naturally. Session 1 described the requirements for a production-ready agent. Session 2 explained the trusted and governed data foundation that such an agent needs. Session 3 expanded the same ideas into a large operational use case in which agents, tools, policies, approval gates, and human teams work together. This progression helped me build a more complete understanding of Agentic AI at both application and organizational levels.
Workshop Briefing The event offered two parallel workshop tracks:
Track A: Build with Kiro: From Spec to Working Application. Track B: Build & Deploy AI Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Using Vibe Coding with Kiro. I selected and participated in Track B.
Track B - Build & Deploy AI Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Using Vibe Coding with Kiro Level: Intermediate to Advanced
Workshop Goals Build an AI agent using Kiro. Develop and extend the agent incrementally through guided steps. Prepare and deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Explore the requirements for moving an AI agent from a prototype toward a cloud-based, production-oriented environment. My Progress and Result I completed approximately half of the guided Track B workshop. I practiced the initial stages of building an AI agent with Kiro and explored the workflow for developing the agent step by step and preparing it for deployment on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
Although I did not complete the full workshop journey, the hands-on session gave me practical exposure to agent development and production-oriented deployment concepts. This result is recorded as partial workshop progress and does not claim that the final deployment was completed.
Hands-on Learning Experience The workshop helped convert the morning’s concepts into a development workflow. Working with Kiro showed me how an AI-assisted environment can guide implementation through context, instructions, and incremental tasks instead of producing an entire solution in one uncontrolled step. I practiced following the workshop sequence, reviewing the generated work, and understanding how the local agent-development process was intended to connect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
Completing only about half of the track was still useful because it revealed the difference between understanding an architecture slide and carrying out the implementation. Each stage depends on correct project context, environment preparation, configuration, and verification. The unfinished portion also gave me a clearer learning target: revisit the remaining steps, complete the AgentCore deployment flow, and verify the agent after deployment rather than treating deployment itself as the final result.
Overall Learning Experience This event was primarily a learning opportunity for me. Beyond the individual AWS services, I gained a broader way of thinking about production systems: start from a real problem, define data and security boundaries, make behavior observable and testable, keep humans involved in high-impact decisions, and choose automation according to the operating environment.
The event also helped me identify subjects for further study, including AgentCore runtime components, memory and evaluation, data contracts, metadata and semantic layers, Cedar-based authorization, MCP integration, and the use of AWS Transform for migration and modernization. Observing how the speakers connected these topics to practical scenarios gave me a useful reference for both future learning and future technical presentations.
Key Takeaways Production AI agents require observability, evaluation, reliable context, security, and governance in addition to model capabilities. AI-ready data must be validated, fresh, traceable, explicitly defined, and protected by appropriate access controls. Agentic AI can support cloud migration and modernization while preserving human approval for important decisions. Kiro and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provide a practical path for building and preparing AI agents for cloud deployment. Completing part of Track B helped me understand the initial agent-development workflow and identify the remaining steps required for a complete deployment. title: Prove It: Agentic Cloud Investigation Series
content:
Event Report: “Prove It: Agentic Cloud Investigation Series” Event Information Organizers: CloudThinker × First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Schedule: September 5, 12, and 19, 2026 · 09:00–12:00 Location: AWS Office, 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Saigon Ward, Ho Chi Minh City Role: Participant and member of Team HCM15 (Tyrex) Format: Three hands-on workshops using read-only AWS and Kubernetes demo environments Event Objectives Learn how to govern an AI Agent before granting it access to a cloud environment. Investigate cloud incidents by testing competing hypotheses and collecting traceable evidence. Practise working with AI Agents under explicit identities, permissions, guardrails, and operating boundaries. Build the ability to defend technical conclusions under time pressure. Produce three portfolio artifacts: Agentic Cloud Review, Incident Report, and Investigation Dossier. Program Principles The program emphasized evidence over confidence. Participants did not provide personal AWS credentials and did not modify infrastructure. The demo environments were read-only: teams could inspect, analyze, investigate, and recommend, but could not execute remediation.
Each session followed the structure LEARN → PRACTICE → SHARE, combining guided concepts, hands-on investigation, and presentation of findings.
Day 01 — GOVERN · Observe Before You Act Saturday, September 5, 2026
Main Activities Examined how the security boundary changes when an AI Agent receives access to a cloud environment. Identified the Agent identity and designed permissions according to the principle of least privilege. Defined operating boundaries and guardrails before granting access. Used a read-only Agent to review an AWS demo account without changing its resources. Recorded observations, risks, and recommended follow-up actions based on evidence. Outcome Understood why Agent governance must be designed before access is enabled. Distinguished read-only observation from permissions that can mutate resources. Practised supervising an Agent instead of automatically accepting its output. Completed the Agentic Cloud Review artifact and developed the Agent Supervisor skill. Reference: Day 01 — GOVERN
Day 02 — INVESTIGATE · From Signal to Root Cause Saturday, September 12, 2026
Main Activities Investigated a cloud environment that had been intentionally misconfigured. Challenged the Agent’s initial answer instead of accepting the first explanation. Developed competing hypotheses and tested them against evidence collected from the environment. Recorded claims, sources, and supporting or contradicting evidence in an Evidence Table. Constructed a Causal Graph connecting the observed symptoms to the underlying cause. Consolidated the investigation into an Incident Report. Outcome Improved the ability to distinguish observations, hypotheses, evidence, and conclusions. Practised rejecting unsupported claims and tracing each conclusion back to its source. Completed the Incident Report artifact and developed the Agentic Incident Investigator skill. Team HCM15 (Tyrex) achieved a score of 93.6/100 for the Day 02 submission. Reference: Day 02 — INVESTIGATE
Day 03 — OPERATE · Prove It Arena Saturday, September 19, 2026
Main Activities Competed in the Prove It Arena as a member of Team HCM15 (Tyrex). Received an unfamiliar cloud environment and performed a rapid initial review. Built an Environment Map covering the main resources, dependencies, access boundaries, and potential risks. Responded to an incident inject under time pressure. Divided responsibilities for Agent operation, competing-hypothesis review, evidence collection, causal analysis, and dossier preparation. Collected evidence with identifiable sources and timestamps, constructed a Causal Graph, and prepared the Investigation Dossier. Defended the team’s conclusions before the judging panel in the Final Defence. Outcome Applied the complete investigation workflow: rapid review, hypothesis development, evidence collection, causal reasoning, decision, and defence. Completed the Investigation Dossier artifact and practised the Agentic Cloud Operator skill. The Day 03 result was below the team’s expectations, revealing areas to improve in role assignment, time management, evidence verification, and technical defence. Reference: Day 03 — Prove It Arena
Arena Evaluation Rubric Agent governance and operating boundaries: 15 points Environment review and risk prioritization: 20 points Incident investigation and causal reasoning: 30 points Decision and remediation quality: 20 points Evidence defence and communication: 15 points Each hint incurred a two-point deduction, and claims without a traceable source received no credit. A conclusion of insufficient evidence could still receive credit when defended appropriately.
Overall Series Results Completed all three stages: GOVERN, INVESTIGATE, and OPERATE. Produced the three portfolio artifacts: Agentic Cloud Review, Incident Report, and Investigation Dossier. Developed the Agent Supervisor, Agentic Incident Investigator, and Agentic Cloud Operator skills. Based on the team’s combined performance across the three days, Team HCM15 (Tyrex) received the award “Most Impressive Submission from Ho Chi Minh City.” Key Takeaways An AI Agent must operate within a clearly defined identity, permission scope, and set of guardrails. The Agent’s first answer is a hypothesis, not a verified conclusion. Every important claim should be traceable to evidence and its source. Competing hypotheses reduce confirmation bias during incident investigation. Effective teamwork requires explicit roles for Agent operation, evidence recording, opposing hypotheses, causal analysis, and report preparation. A technically reasonable conclusion is not enough unless the team can communicate and defend it clearly. Event Experience The series provided a practical view of how AI Agents can support cloud operations without replacing human judgement. The most valuable lesson was to treat confidence as insufficient and require evidence before accepting a conclusion. Working with Team HCM15 (Tyrex) also highlighted the importance of role clarity, time management, and communication during an investigation.
Although the Day 03 performance did not meet the team’s expectations, the experience exposed concrete weaknesses that can be improved in future incident-response exercises. Completing the full series helped connect cloud governance, investigation, and operations into one evidence-driven workflow.

title: Prerequisites and Deployment
content:
Prerequisites and Deployment Tools Tool Check .NET SDK 10 dotnet --list-sdks AWS CLI v2, signed in, region ap-southeast-1 aws sts get-caller-identity AWS SAM CLI (a version that supports the dotnet10 runtime) sam --version Amazon.Lambda.Tools dotnet tool install -g Amazon.Lambda.Tools Python 3.10+ (prepares the Olist data) python --version I chose .NET 10 because Lambda’s dotnet8 runtime reached end of support on 10 November 2026, and dotnet10 is the current long-term-support version.
Step 1 - Build and Test Locally git clone https://github.com/Viluoicode/ontime-radar.git cd ontime-radar dotnet build dotnet test The tests need no AWS account and no Docker. The service tests use small in-memory fakes of DynamoDB, SQS, S3, and Athena (see 5.1.6).
Step 2 - First Deployment From Your Machine Copy-Item samconfig.example.toml samconfig.toml sam build sam deploy --guided The guided deploy asks for these parameters:
Parameter What to enter WebhookSecret a random string of at least 16 characters; carriers send it in a header AlertEmail the address that receives alarms ReplayState DISABLED for now; turn it on after testing OrdersPerRun 20 orders per 15-minute run LateRatePercent 20: alarm when 20% or more of deliveries are late MinDeliveries 10: a 15-minute window counts only with at least 10 deliveries samconfig.toml holds the webhook secret, so it is listed in .gitignore.

$pool = "<UserPoolId>" aws cognito-idp admin-create-user --user-pool-id $pool --username staff@example.com ` --user-attributes Name=email,Value=staff@example.com Name=email_verified,Value=true aws cognito-idp admin-add-user-to-group --user-pool-id $pool --username staff@example.com --group-name cskh Use the group manager for an account that should also see the SLA reports.

At 20 orders every 15 minutes, the replay sends about 1,900 orders a day and lasts about 50 days.

In GitHub, create an environment named production with Required reviewers turned on, limited to the main branch. Add the deploy role ARN as the environment secret AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN. This is a role name, not an access key. From then on, each push to main that changes code runs: tests → wait for approval → assume the role through OIDC → sam deploy → upload the website → check /health. title: Project Proposal
content:
Project Proposal - OnTime Radar (Shipment SLA Service) 1. Summary OnTime Radar is a serverless service on AWS for online shops that ship through several carriers. It receives status webhooks from every carrier, turns them into one trustworthy timeline per shipment, warns staff by email when deliveries start running late, and reports the on-time rate per carrier and region. A web dashboard with login gives customer service and managers what each of them needs.
The project runs on real traffic. A scheduled job replays about 98,000 historical orders from the public Olist e-commerce dataset as carrier webhooks, every 15 minutes, so the system is tested on realistic volume rather than a few hand-made requests.
This is my second internship project. The first one, Job Market AWS Pipeline (a batch data pipeline), is kept in the Workshop as an additional case study.
2. Problem A small or medium online shop in Vietnam often uses two to four carriers at the same time. Every carrier uses its own status codes, its own tracking website, and its own webhook format. The shop pays for this every day:
Pain Consequence Staff check several carrier websites to track one order slow answers to customers A late parcel is noticed only when the customer complains bad reviews and returns There is no on-time data per carrier or region carriers are chosen by feel, and there is nothing to negotiate with Webhooks arrive twice or in the wrong order the order status jumps backwards and staff stop trusting it 3. Objectives and Success Criteria Objectives Accept webhooks from three carriers (GHN, GHTK, J&T; simulated formats) and map them onto one set of eight statuses. Process each shipment’s events in order, ignore duplicates, and refuse impossible status changes. Give a full shipment timeline in one API call. Detect a rising late-delivery rate and email the operations team. Report the on-time rate by carrier, region, and week. Provide a web dashboard with two roles: customer service and manager. Deploy everything as code, automatically, without long-lived access keys. Success criteria Criterion How it is checked No wrong final status when events are duplicated or shuffled Chaos test against the deployed API: 0 differences from an independent answer key No event lost Replayer Failed = 0; dead-letter queue empty A late-delivery problem reaches a person without anyone watching a screen Alarm → SNS email, tested with the demo script A customer-service account cannot see management reports 401/403 permission matrix checked on the live API Reports cost little to run Athena query cap of 1 GB; cache hit rate measured The system can be rebuilt and removed from code One SAM template; documented cleanup 4. Proposed Architecture The system has three flows:
Events in: carrier webhook → API Gateway → Lambda adapter → SQS FIFO (one group per shipment) → Lambda processor → DynamoDB (status + history in one transaction) and an S3 event lake. Staff dashboard: browser → CloudFront → private S3 website; sign-in with Cognito; API Gateway checks the token; lookups read DynamoDB, and reports run in Athena over the event lake. Alerts: processor metrics → CloudWatch alarm on the late rate and on the dead-letter queue → SNS email. Deployment: GitHub Actions runs the tests, waits for my approval, gets a temporary role through OIDC, and runs sam deploy.
5. AWS Services and Why Service Role in the system Why this one Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) entry point for webhooks and the dashboard JWT check, throttling, and CORS without a server AWS Lambda (.NET 10, arm64) adapters, processor, replayer pay per use; arm64 is about 20% cheaper Amazon SQS FIFO + DLQ keep each shipment’s events in order ordering per message group, with parallel groups Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand) current status and history transactions and conditional writes for idempotency Amazon S3 event lake, dataset, website files cheap and durable AWS Glue Data Catalog + Amazon Athena SLA reports with SQL no database server; partition projection, so no crawler Amazon EventBridge Scheduler runs the replayer every 15 minutes simple managed schedule Amazon Cognito staff login and roles managed sign-in, groups, and optional MFA Amazon CloudFront serves the dashboard over HTTPS keeps the bucket private through OAC, adds security headers Amazon CloudWatch + Amazon SNS metrics, logs, alarms, email built-in and cheap at this scale AWS IAM + AWS SAM / CloudFormation permissions and infrastructure as code least privilege, a permissions boundary, and repeatable deploys 6. Security and Operations Staff log in through Cognito (authorization code + PKCE). The gateway rejects bad tokens (401), and the Lambda rejects the wrong role (403). Carriers authenticate with a webhook secret. Input is validated, and bad input gets 400. The website bucket is private, CloudFront adds HSTS, CSP, and other security headers, and only GET requests from the dashboard’s own domain are allowed by CORS. Every role carries a permissions boundary. Deployments use OIDC with an approval step, and no access key is stored anywhere. API throttling of 10 requests per second per route protects the account’s Lambda concurrency. A daily health-check script and two alarms cover the replayer, queues, Lambdas, the event lake, the API, and the website. 7. Timeline The project started on 16 November 2026 (Week 21). Workshop submission is due by 16 December.
Week Dates Work Status 21 16/11 – 22/11 Webhooks, FIFO processing, DynamoDB, S3 lake, replayer, Athena reports, Cognito, dashboard on CloudFront, alarms, CI/CD through OIDC, security review fixes Done 22 23/11 – 27/11 Chaos testing against the deployed API, known limitations, evidence collection In progress 23 30/11 – 04/12 Cost report (Cost Explorer + Pricing Calculator), demo video Planned 24 07/12 – 11/12 Final workshop review, report, and submission Planned 8. Budget With the replayer sending about 1,900 orders (about 9,000 events) a day, the early estimate is USD 3–5 per month, mostly DynamoDB writes. The design keeps cost low with serverless services on arm64, on-demand DynamoDB, no VPC or NAT gateway, a 1 GB cap per Athena query, a two-layer report cache, and 14-day log retention.
This is an estimate, not a bill. The final report will include measured Cost Explorer figures and a saved AWS Pricing Calculator estimate based on them.
9. Risks and Mitigations Risk Mitigation Duplicate or out-of-order webhooks FIFO per shipment, deterministic event IDs, version check, and status rules A message that keeps failing Partial batch failure; after 5 attempts it goes to the DLQ, which raises an alarm A traffic burst uses all Lambda capacity (10 in a new account) API throttling and a processor concurrency limit; a quota increase is planned Alert fatigue Alarm on a sustained late rate, not a raw count A leaked deploy credential No stored keys; OIDC bound to repository IDs and the approved environment; permissions boundary An expensive runaway query Athena workgroup cap of 1 GB per query Misleading numbers Demo and test shipments are excluded; limitations of the simulated fields and the Brazilian data are documented AI-generated code that is wrong Code review, more than 200 automated tests including mutation checks, and a chaos test on the live system 10. Deliverables Source code, the SAM template, and the CI/CD workflows in the ontime-radar repository. Architecture diagram (draw.io, AWS icons). A running system with the web dashboard, alarms, and daily replay. A bilingual Workshop with deployment, testing, cost, and cleanup steps. Evidence: daily-check outputs, a chaos test report, and screenshots. A demo video (in progress). A cost report (in progress).

title: Prerequisites and Environment
content:
Prerequisites and Environment Required Tools An AWS account with permission to create the project resources. AWS CLI configured with short-lived or otherwise approved credentials. Terraform 1.10 or newer (the S3 state lock needs it). Python 3.11 for the local test suite. Java 17 for local PySpark tests. Git and a terminal. A browser for the AWS Console and Streamlit dashboard. The deployment region is ap-southeast-1. Credentials, Terraform state, real .tfvars, email addresses, and downloaded source data must not be committed.
Repository Preparation git clone https://github.com/Viluoicode/Job-Market-Pipeline-cloud.git cd Job-Market-Pipeline-cloud python -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt Validate Before Deployment terraform -chdir=infra init -backend=false terraform -chdir=infra fmt -check -recursive terraform -chdir=infra validate python -m pytest tests -q Local tests mock public APIs and AWS clients. Passing locally is necessary but does not replace evidence from an AWS deployment.
Terraform Configuration Copy infra/terraform.tfvars.example to a private, uncommitted configuration file and review:
Region and project name. Schedule enablement and cron expression. Alert email and monitoring subscription. Glue worker type, worker count, and timeout. Ingestion and monitoring success thresholds. Freshness and lifecycle thresholds. Dashboard reader principal ARNs. Bucket cleanup behavior. Deploy with Terraform Step 1 - Create the state bucket (once) Terraform keeps its state in an S3 bucket that I create by hand, outside the stack. Keeping it outside means terraform destroy can never delete the state that describes the stack.
$account = aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text $stateBucket = "jobmarket-aws-tfstate-$account-ap-southeast-1" aws s3api create-bucket --bucket $stateBucket --region ap-southeast-1 ` --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=ap-southeast-1 aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket $stateBucket --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket $stateBucket --public-access-block-configuration ` BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true "bucket = `"$stateBucket`"" | Set-Content -Encoding utf8 infra/backend.hcl backend.hcl contains the account ID, so it stays out of Git.
Step 2 - Plan and apply terraform -chdir=infra init -backend-config=backend.hcl terraform -chdir=infra plan -out=workshop.tfplan terraform -chdir=infra apply workshop.tfplan Read the plan before you apply it: it lists every bucket, Glue job, IAM role, and alarm that will start costing money. Keep enable_schedule = false for the first deployment so nothing runs until you have checked it by hand.
📷 Screenshot to add: the Apply complete! summary with the resource count.
Step 3 - Run the pipeline once by hand $pipelineArn = terraform -chdir=infra output -raw state_machine_arn aws stepfunctions start-execution --state-machine-arn $pipelineArn --region ap-southeast-1 A full run takes roughly ten minutes.
Step 4 - Check the result In the AWS Console (region Singapore):
Step Functions: the execution ends in SUCCEEDED and every stage is green. S3 → lake bucket: state/pipeline/latest.json exists and names the run you just started. S3: open control/ingestion/run_id=<run>/manifest.json and look at the board counts. DynamoDB → lock table: the table is empty, so the lock was released. Athena: a count query on fact_job_posting returns rows for today’s snapshot. You can also run the same freshness check from the terminal:
$lake = terraform -chdir=infra output -raw lake_bucket python scripts/check_freshness.py --bucket $lake --region ap-southeast-1 📷 Screenshots to add: the Step Functions graph, the manifest in S3, and the Athena query result.
Step 5 - Turn on the daily schedule When the manual run passes every check, set enable_schedule = true in terraform.tfvars, run plan and apply again, and confirm in EventBridge → Rules that the pipeline rule shows ENABLED. From then on the pipeline runs every day at 18:00 UTC (01:00 in Vietnam).
Security Preparation Use an authenticated deployment identity only for intentional infrastructure changes. The dashboard must assume its dedicated restricted reader role; an administrator credential must not be used as an implicit dashboard fallback.

title: Project 1 - Job Market AWS Pipeline
content:
Job Market AWS Pipeline Overview Job Market AWS Pipeline is an AWS data-engineering workshop that collects job postings from public APIs, preserves traceable observations in a data lake, transforms them through Bronze, Silver, and Gold layers, and exposes the published results through Amazon Athena and a local Streamlit dashboard.
The project addresses a practical problem: public job platforms use different schemas, sources can fail or return incomplete results, and a posting may change or disappear over time. A successful download script alone cannot prove that the resulting data is current, complete, deduplicated, or safe to publish.
Project History A first prototype was started in late June 2026, before the internship began. During the internship (Weeks 13-24), it was re-scoped, redesigned, hardened, and deployed on AWS with Terraform, Data Quality gates, orchestration, monitoring, and tests.
Project Goals Collect a configured sample of job postings every day without depending on a personal computer. Preserve source observations and a committed manifest for traceability. Normalize data and track posting lifecycle in the Silver layer. Enforce data-quality checks before advancing published state. Produce queryable Gold data products for job, role, company, location, and remote analysis. Automate the workflow and prevent overlapping writers. Monitor freshness and source coverage independently of the main pipeline. Provide a dashboard that refuses stale, incomplete, or in-progress publication. Scope The configured sample contains 36 boards across Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, and Arbeitnow. The system is designed as an educational, portfolio-scale batch pipeline. It does not claim to represent the whole job market, recommend jobs to an individual, or determine whether every posting is still available on the employer website.
Main AWS Services Amazon S3 AWS Glue Python Shell and AWS Glue Spark AWS Step Functions Amazon EventBridge Amazon DynamoDB AWS Glue Data Catalog (Gold tables in Apache Iceberg format) Amazon Athena AWS Lambda Amazon CloudWatch Amazon SNS AWS IAM AI-Assisted Development AI tools supported research, implementation suggestions, code review, testing ideas, and documentation. I remained responsible for defining the project requirements, reviewing architectural decisions, validating the proposed code, checking AWS behavior, troubleshooting failures, testing the pipeline, and documenting verified results.
Workshop Sections Architecture and design decisions Prerequisites and environment preparation Multi-source ingestion and Bronze storage Silver lifecycle, Data Quality, and Gold marts Orchestration, security, and monitoring Dashboard, testing, and verified results Cost, cleanup, limitations, and reflection Troubleshooting and future work Current Evidence From 15 September to 21 November 2026, all 68 scheduled nightly runs succeeded. The snapshot of 21 November held 8,672 open postings from 467 employers, collected from 36 of 36 boards. These numbers describe a past point in time; section 5.2.6 explains how to check the pipeline’s current state.

title: Ingestion and Bronze Layer
content:
Ingestion and Bronze Layer The Boards ingestion/sources.json lists 36 boards on four platforms:
Platform Boards Examples Greenhouse 20 Stripe, Airbnb, Databricks, GitLab Ashby 11 OpenAI, Notion, Ramp, Mistral AI Lever 4 Spotify, Palantir Arbeitnow 1 a feed that aggregates many companies None of them needs an API key. A test checks that the list is well formed: every platform is supported, no board appears twice, and no company is listed on two platforms. That last rule exists because Mistral AI moved from Lever to Ashby in November (see 5.2.8).
Step 1 - Fetch the Boards in Parallel The job runs five API calls at a time. Each call has a 20-second timeout and up to three attempts. It retries on network errors, HTTP 429, and 5xx responses, and it waits longer after each failure.
Results are processed in the same order as the list, whichever call finishes first. The job only fetches up to ten boards ahead of what it has already written. That limit matters because a single run produces about 150 MB of JSON, and Glue Python Shell has about 1 GB of memory.
Step 2 - Turn Every Answer Into the Same Shape Each platform names its fields differently. A small adapter per platform maps them into one record: source, board, the platform’s job ID, company, title, location, work mode, application URL, posting date, and the original JSON.
Work mode has three values: remote, onsite or hybrid, and unknown. Each platform gives a different hint (Lever and Ashby have a workplace type, Arbeitnow has a remote flag, Greenhouse only has the location text). When no hint is present, the value stays unknown instead of being guessed. On 20 November, 47.5% of postings were unknown.
If a response does not look like a list of jobs, the board is marked as failed. It is never treated as a board that simply had no jobs.
Step 3 - Write Bronze, Then the Manifest Each board’s records go to their own file, under a folder for the run:
bronze/run_id=<run>/source=<platform>/board=<token>/jobs.json Only after every board has been handled does the job write the manifest:
control/ingestion/run_id=<run>/manifest.json The manifest puts each board in one of four groups: success with records, success but empty, failed, or incomplete (Arbeitnow is read two pages deep, so it is always incomplete). The run succeeds only when at least 80% of boards succeed and at least one posting was collected.
The manifest works as the commit point. If the job crashes halfway, the files it already wrote are never read, because no manifest lists them. If S3 itself refuses a write, the whole run stops: a storage problem must not be recorded as a broken job board.
Step 4 - Check It After a run, open the manifest in S3 and compare the board counts with the source-coverage-low alarm in CloudWatch. 36 of 36 successful boards means full coverage. Arbeitnow is still reported as incomplete because of the page limit, which is expected.
📷 Screenshot to add: a manifest file open in the S3 console, with the board counts visible.

title: Receiving and Processing Events
content:
Receiving and Processing Events One Adapter per Carrier The three carriers use different payloads. The formats are simulated in this project, not the carriers’ official specifications:
Carrier Example field Example value GHN text status delivering GHTK numeric status status_id = 45 J&T scan type scanType = DELIVERY Each adapter is one class that turns its carrier’s payload into the same event: carrier, tracking code, common status, time it happened, promised delivery date, and region. Adding a carrier means adding one class; the rest of the pipeline does not change.
The adapters also check their input. A tracking code must match ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$, because it becomes part of a DynamoDB key, a URL, and an S3 path. A payload with the wrong shape is answered with 400, so the carrier does not keep retrying it.
The Eight Statuses CREATED → PICKED_UP → IN_TRANSIT (repeats between hubs) → OUT_FOR_DELIVERY → DELIVERED ↕ FAILED_ATTEMPT → RETURNED CREATED → CANCELLED Keeping Each Shipment in Order The API Lambda puts each event on an SQS FIFO queue with MessageGroupId set to the shipment, then answers 202 straight away. FIFO delivers the events of one shipment strictly in order, while other shipments are processed in parallel.
The eventId is a hash of the event’s content. If a carrier sends the same webhook twice, both copies get the same ID. SQS drops a copy that arrives within five minutes, and DynamoDB catches any later one.
Deciding What an Event Means The processor compares each event with what it already knows about the shipment:
Situation Outcome Effect Same eventId seen before Duplicate nothing is written Happened earlier than the latest applied event Stale kept in history, status unchanged Shipment already finished (delivered, returned, cancelled) Rejected kept in history, status unchanged Moves backwards, e.g. in transit after out for delivery Rejected kept in history, status unchanged Anything else Applied status updated A shipment counts as late when the delivery date is after the promised date.
Writing the Result The status item and the history item are written to DynamoDB in a single transaction, with a version check, so they can never disagree and two writers cannot overwrite each other. The table uses one partition per shipment, so a single query returns the status together with the whole history.
The processor then:
appends the event to s3://<data bucket>/events/dt=YYYY-MM-DD/ as JSON lines, for Athena; publishes Deliveries and LateDeliveries metrics to CloudWatch, per carrier. The SQS trigger uses partial batch failure. If one message fails, that message and every later message in the same group go back to the queue, and nothing after the failure is processed out of order. After five failed attempts, a message moves to the dead-letter queue, which triggers an alarm.
The Replayer Every 15 minutes EventBridge Scheduler runs the Replayer Lambda. It reads the next 20 Olist orders from S3, turns each order into a series of carrier webhooks, and sends them to the public API, exactly like a real carrier would.
A cursor in DynamoDB remembers where the replay stopped. The cursor moves forward only when no webhook failed for a temporary reason (throttling, 5xx, or network), so the next run sends the same orders again. Copies that were already processed come back as Duplicate.
Try It $api = "<ApiUrl>" $h = @{ "X-Webhook-Secret" = "<WebhookSecret>" } Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$api/carriers/ghn/webhook" -Headers $h -ContentType "application/json" -InFile tools/sample-webhook-ghn.json Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post "$api/carriers/ghn/webhook" -Headers $h -ContentType "application/json" -InFile tools/sample-webhook-ghn-delivered.json Start-Sleep 5 Invoke-RestMethod "$api/shipments/ghn/GHNTEST001" -Headers $auth | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5 The shipment ends as Delivered and isLate = true, with two Applied events. Sending the first webhook again adds nothing, and a wrong secret returns 401. $auth holds a Cognito token (see 5.1.5).

title: First Cloud AI Journey: Community Day
content:
First Cloud AI Journey: Community Day Event Information Date: Saturday, October 31, 2026 Location: Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Organizer: AWS Study Group / First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) community Role: Attendee Format: Six morning sessions by industry speakers and FCAJ interns Event Overview Community Day brought together the First Cloud AI Journey community, where working engineers and program interns shared hands-on experience with AWS. Unlike the two previous events, the agenda did not focus on a single service or use case. It followed the path of a cloud learner: getting started with AWS, bringing AI into the software development process, building serverless applications, re-architecting web workloads, handling asynchronous processing, and contributing to open source.
Session 1 - AWS Roadmap for Beginners Speaker: Minh Tuấn - Backend Developer, FCAJ intern
The opening session introduced a structured, low-cost path for beginners to learn AWS.
AWS Study Group: step-by-step hands-on labs in Vietnamese, regularly updated by community admins. AWS Skill Builder: role-based learning plans, labs, and certification preparation, such as AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner. AWS Builder Center: reading and writing technical articles, joining hackathons and Student Builder Groups. AWS Cloud Quest: game-based 3D learning with free courses such as Cloud Practitioner and AI Foundations. Student benefits: student verification for a Skill Builder Subscription (worth about $449/year) and certification vouchers earned through Builder Center badges; new accounts can also claim free credits. The speaker stressed a safe lab workflow: understand the service → experiment → troubleshoot (ask AI or admins) → always clean up resources afterwards to avoid unexpected charges.
What I valued most was treating clean-up as a required step of every lab rather than an optional extra. It is a habit I need to keep when deploying personal projects on my own AWS account.
Session 2 - Lessons from Building a Software Factory with AI Speaker: Henry Đức Bùi - Head of Engineering, CloudThinker
This session showed how a small team organizes its software delivery process around AI coding agents.
Results: a team of 5-6 people handled nearly 3,000 merge requests (MRs) in one month, about 100 per day, most of them executed and merged by AI. The new bottleneck is people: once token budget is no longer the constraint, the limit becomes how many parallel agents humans can review and approve. Discuss before coding: about 60% of the time goes to AI-assisted discussion, ending with HTML dashboards or diagrams generated by AI for the team to review and agree on. Divergent prompting: avoid narrow prompts and leave room for the AI to suggest alternatives (for example, adding “feel free to advise me”). “Folder Control” pattern: a single control folder with an agent.md file of basic instructions so agents can coordinate across multiple repositories and servers. Automated review and merge: most small MRs, such as maintenance, refactoring, security checks, and performance tuning, are checked, debated, and merged by agents. Verification by evidence: AI must run end-to-end tests and provide before/after screenshots or screen recordings of test runs. CI/CD optimization: run CI on local or dedicated high-spec servers, cache test results (cutting test time by about 76%), and share dependency environments. This session connected directly to the evidence over confidence principle from the Prove It series (Event 1): AI output is accepted only when backed by tests, screenshots, or recordings. I also realized that as AI writes code faster, reviewing, writing clear requirements, and designing verification steps become more important skills.
Session 3 - Three-Month Internship Journey: Building a Real-time Serverless Web Game Speaker: Phúc Khang - FCAJ intern (Software Engineering)
The speaker presented a real-time multiplayer card game built during a three-month internship.
Tech stack: AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon SQS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon API Gateway (WebSocket and HTTP), Amazon Cognito, AWS Amplify, and AWS CDK. Four serverless patterns: Synchronous: API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB for authentication and basic reads/writes. Scheduled job: periodic leaderboard updates. Asynchronous filtering: EventBridge for asynchronous event handling. Message queue: SQS as a buffer for match results so the database is not overwhelmed when many results arrive at once. Lessons from real incidents:
Using SQS as a turn timer caused polling between Lambda and SQS to generate about 863,000 requests with no players online, exceeding the Free Tier. The team switched to EventBridge as a “watchdog” for timeouts and AFK detection. Do not put all permissions into a single IAM role, as it violates least privilege. Do not store secrets directly in Lambda environment variables; use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store or AWS Secrets Manager with AWS KMS. Move from manual AWS Console changes to Infrastructure as Code with AWS CDK and AWS CloudFormation. This was the session closest to my own situation as an intern. The 863,000-request incident showed that a service used for the wrong purpose can cost money even with zero users, and that budget alerts and metrics should be set up from day one, even for small projects.
Session 4 - Re-architecting Web Applications with AWS Lambda Web Adapter Speaker: Thịnh Nguyễn - DevOps / Cloud Engineer, Style Solution
This session compared running web applications on traditional Lambda functions with packaging the whole web app as a container image and running it on Lambda through the Lambda Web Adapter.
Limitations of the traditional approach for web apps:
Each request occupies an execution environment, causing cold-start spikes during sudden traffic bursts. Dependence on API Gateway adds latency and cost. Billing includes time spent waiting for database I/O. Proposed approach:
Package the web app (Express.js, FastAPI, …) as a Docker container image (up to 10 GB) and deploy it to Lambda. According to the speaker, one execution environment can handle many concurrent requests (up to 128), so cold starts mainly affect the first request. Route from Amazon CloudFront to a Lambda Function URL using Origin Access Control (OAC), without API Gateway and without exposing a public endpoint. The speaker estimated a 40-70% reduction in compute cost because I/O wait time is not billed. Selection criteria:
Traditional Lambda: small, single-purpose tasks such as generating S3 presigned URLs, sending notifications, or cron jobs. Lambda with Web Adapter: full-stack web applications or complete API backends. This session showed me that serverless does not require one function per route. For a .NET backend, I can consider packaging an entire ASP.NET Core API as a container image and compare the trade-offs with splitting it into separate functions.
Session 5 - Asynchronous Processing with Amazon SQS Speaker: Cẩm Đào - FCAJ intern
This session explained why long-running tasks such as AI model calls should move from synchronous to asynchronous processing.
Synchronous: the user calls the API and waits until Amazon Bedrock finishes generating the result. Asynchronous: the user submits a job → the API immediately returns a Pending status → the job is stored in SQS → an AI worker picks it up and processes it in the background. Choosing a queue type:
Standard queue: very high throughput, but message order is not guaranteed. FIFO queue: guaranteed ordering per message group ID, at lower throughput. Safe message handling:
Visibility timeout and heartbeat: a received message is hidden for the visibility timeout; for long tasks, the consumer must extend it to prevent duplicate processing. Long polling: set a wait time (for example, 20 seconds) when the queue is empty to reduce unnecessary requests and cost. Dead-letter queue (DLQ): keep messages that exceed the retry limit for later inspection without blocking the main flow. Fan-out with SNS + SQS: one message published to Amazon SNS is delivered to multiple SQS queues for logging or parallel processing. This content applies directly to my logistics projects, where shipment events need asynchronous processing. I noted three checks for SQS: the visibility timeout must exceed processing time, a DLQ must be configured, and consumers must be idempotent because messages can be delivered more than once.
Session 6 - Staying Persistent: Open Source Contribution with AWS CDK Speaker: Hưng Trần - Senior Cloud Engineer, NAB; Top 25 AWS CDK Contributor
The final session described the reality of contributing to large open-source projects such as Kubernetes, Terraform, and AWS CDK, where a pull request (PR) can take 6 to 8 months to be reviewed.
A three-stage contributor roadmap:
0 → 1 PR: look for good first issue labels or join large refactoring campaigns where maintainers provide templates and checklists; keep PRs small and simple. 1 → 20 PRs: try several repositories to find the project and maintainer team that fit best. 20+ PRs: find your own work, for example by checking the AWS What’s New page daily and updating CDK, Terraform, or Pulumi when AWS launches a new feature or region. Core mindset: spend about 15 minutes a day on small tasks such as version upgrades, and do not wait to read all documentation or understand the whole architecture before starting; the fastest way to learn is to fix a concrete issue.
This session changed how I see open source: it does not start with a large contribution but with consistency and patience. It is also a practical way to build a publicly verifiable portfolio.
Learning from the Speakers and Session Structure What made Community Day different was that half of the speakers were interns. Intern sessions focused on concrete incidents, measurable numbers, and fixes, while industry speakers offered perspectives on process, cost, and long-term mindset. The two viewpoints complemented each other.
Presentation techniques I want to apply when sharing my own projects:
Tell real incidents with concrete numbers (requests, cost, time) instead of only describing an ideal architecture. Show “before and after” when changing an architecture so the trade-offs are visible. Give clear selection criteria (when to use A, when to use B) rather than presenting one solution as always right. End with small actions the audience can take immediately. Overall Learning Experience The event helped me review the whole cloud learning journey from the perspective of people one step ahead. The sessions on serverless, Lambda Web Adapter, and SQS provided patterns I can apply to my current projects; the Software Factory session showed how AI is changing the way engineering teams work; and the sessions on open source and the beginner roadmap reminded me that progress comes from small, consistent actions.
After the event, I identified several items to practise: trying Lambda Web Adapter with a containerized .NET API, adding DLQs and tuning visibility timeouts for the queues in my projects, reviewing IAM roles and secret storage, and finding a good first issue in the AWS CDK repository to start contributing.
Key Takeaways Always clean up resources and monitor cost when running labs or personal projects on AWS. AI can greatly increase development throughput, but its output must be verified with tests and concrete evidence. Choose services for the right purpose: misusing SQS can generate hundreds of thousands of unnecessary requests; EventBridge fits time-based monitoring better. Apply least privilege to IAM, store secrets in Parameter Store or Secrets Manager, and manage infrastructure as code. Lambda Web Adapter is worth considering for running a full web app on Lambda with lower cost and fewer cold starts. Asynchronous processing with SQS needs a suitable visibility timeout, long polling, a DLQ, and idempotent consumers. Open-source contribution starts with small PRs and requires months of persistence. title: Silver, Data Quality, and Gold
content:
Silver, Data Quality, and Gold Bronze to Silver The Silver job reads only the files named in this run’s manifest. Before it starts, it checks that the manifest belongs to the same run and UTC date, that the run succeeded, and that the manifest is recent.
Giving Each Posting an Identity job_id is a SHA-256 hash of platform, board, and the platform’s job ID. The board is part of the key because two employers on the same platform can reuse the same internal ID. dedup_hash is built from the normalized company, title, and location. Gold uses it to spot the same job posted on two platforms. Deciding Whether a Posting Is Still Open The job compares today’s observations with the previous Silver run:
What happened today What Silver records The posting was seen Keep the first-seen time, update last-seen, mark active The board answered completely and the posting was missing Closed: missing from a complete board The board failed or was cut short Keep the last observation: the board could not be verified Not seen for seven days Closed: the observation is too old A closed posting appears again Reopen it and keep the original first-seen time The key rule is that a broken board never closes anything. If Lever is down for a day, its postings keep their last observation, instead of looking like a wave of closures.
Data Quality Gate Before Silver is published, Glue Data Quality checks seven rules:
There is at least one row. Every row has a job_id. No job_id appears twice. Every row has a dedup_hash. At least 30% of rows have a known work mode. The threshold is low because many boards do not state it. The platform is one of the four supported ones. At least 90% of rows have a company name. If any rule fails, the run stops and the previous Silver stays the published one. Only after the rules pass does the job write the new run and move state/silver/latest.json to point at it.
Silver to Gold Gold keeps postings that are active and were seen within the freshness window. Three tables are built:
Table One row per Used for fact_job_posting unique open posting browsing jobs, companies, locations, work mode, and apply links demand_by_role role family per day comparing demand between roles role_opportunity role family per day demand rank, remote share, and the top employer for each role When the same job appears on two platforms, Gold keeps the most recently seen copy, then the one with a posting date, then the lowest job_id, so the choice is always the same.
Role Families Each title is matched against 15 role families in a fixed priority order, for example Forward Deployed / Solutions, ML / AI Engineer, Data Engineer, DevOps / SRE, Backend Engineer, and finally Software Engineer (General). A posting gets at most one family, so the counts add up. Titles such as recruiter or account executive are excluded on purpose. On 20 November about 60% of postings matched no family, mostly sales, legal, and hardware jobs. They stay in the totals but not in the role charts.
Writing Gold as Iceberg Each table is an Apache Iceberg table under gold_iceberg/ in the lake bucket. A run replaces exactly one snapshot_date per table in a single commit, even when the result is empty, so a reader sees either yesterday’s version or today’s, never a half-written day.
The job then writes a small record with the new snapshot ID of each table. Step Functions checks that this record belongs to the current run and copies the three IDs into the completion marker. Readers query FOR VERSION AS OF <snapshot id>, so all three tables are read at the same point in time.
Before switching, I ran Iceberg in “shadow” mode next to the old Parquet tables for several days and compared them row by row (see 5.2.8, problem 4). The old Parquet tables are kept, read-only, as history.

title: SLA Reports With Athena
content:
SLA Reports With Athena The Event Lake Every processed event is stored in the data bucket as one JSON line, in a folder per processing day:
s3://<data bucket>/events/dt=2026-11-23/....jsonl The SAM template creates a Glue database shipment_sla_lake and a table events over this folder. The table uses partition projection on dt: Athena works out the folder for each day from the query itself. New data can be queried as soon as it lands, with no crawler and no MSCK REPAIR.
A dedicated Athena workgroup, shipment-sla-wg, stops any single query after it has scanned 1 GB, so a mistake cannot become an expensive bill.
Querying by Hand In the Athena console, choose the workgroup shipment-sla-wg and run, for example:
SELECT carrier, count(*) AS delivered, count_if(islate) AS late FROM shipment_sla_lake.events WHERE dt >= '2026-11-01' AND status = 'Delivered' AND outcome = 'Applied' GROUP BY carrier; Filtering on dt keeps the scan to the days you ask for.
📷 Screenshot to add: this query and its result in the Athena console, with the scanned size visible.
Report API The dashboard does not run SQL itself. It calls these endpoints:
Endpoint Who can call it Returns GET /sla/summary?days=&groupBy=carrier|region manager delivered, late, and late % per carrier or region GET /sla/trend?days=&carrier= manager per delivery day: orders, late %, average delivery time GET /shipments?days=&status=&carrier=&region=&late=&overdue=&limit= customer service + manager a filtered list of shipments GET /shipments/{carrier}/{tracking} customer service + manager one shipment with its full timeline User input never goes into the SQL text. groupBy must be one of two fixed words, and days must be a whole number, which rules out SQL injection. An invalid parameter returns 400 with the reason. Demo shipments (codes starting with DEMO) are left out of the SLA numbers.
Caching The data changes only every 15 minutes, when the replayer runs. Re-running the same query on every page load would waste time and money, so there are two cache layers:
The Lambda keeps each result in memory for 5 minutes. Athena’s query result reuse returns a previous result for up to 15 minutes without scanning S3. I measured 38 queries on 20 November 2026:
Path Time Full scan of S3 about 2.4 s Result reused by Athena about 0.55 s Lambda memory about 0 ms 79% of the queries did not have to scan S3.
Measured Numbers On 19 November 2026, with about 5,700 of the 98,202 Olist orders replayed, the dashboard showed 5,425 delivered orders, a 96.4% on-time rate, and an average delivery time of 13.3 days.
These numbers reflect how the replay works: orders are sent by order date, so the early orders from 2016–2017 dominate. They are not the late rate of the Olist dataset as a whole.
