title: Dashboard, Login, and Security
content:
Dashboard, Login, and Security The Website The dashboard is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (about 90 KB, no build step), with Chart.js for charts. It has a light and a dark theme and also works on a phone. There are three pages:
Page Who sees it What it shows SLA overview manager on-time rate, late rate per week, per carrier, and the regions with the most late deliveries Shipment lookup customer service + manager current status and the full timeline of one shipment Needs attention customer service + manager late, failed-attempt, and overdue shipments, filtered by carrier and region SLA overview, 19 November 2026. The signed-in email is replaced with an example address.
Looking up one shipment. Blocked events are shown with the reason they did not change the status.
The “needs attention” list. Clicking a row opens that shipment’s timeline.
Login and Roles Staff sign in through the Cognito hosted page, using the authorization code flow with PKCE, so the browser holds no client secret. The token is kept only in the browser tab (sessionStorage) and expires after one hour. Multi-factor authentication is optional, and each person can turn it on.
Request No token Token, no group cskh manager GET /shipments... 401 403 ✅ ✅ GET /sla/summary, GET /sla/trend 401 403 403 ✅ The checks happen in two layers:
The API Gateway JWT authorizer stops a missing, invalid, or expired token with 401, before any Lambda runs. API Gateway cannot check Cognito groups, so the Lambda does it and returns 403 for the wrong role. A unit test fails if any GET route except /health is left without a role check. Carrier webhooks do not use Cognito. They must send the X-Webhook-Secret header.
Protecting the Website The web files sit in their own private S3 bucket, separate from the order data. Only CloudFront can read it, through Origin Access Control. CloudFront forces HTTPS and adds security headers: Content-Security-Policy with frame-ancestors 'none', HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and Referrer-Policy: no-referrer. Chart.js is loaded with Subresource Integrity, and every value from the API is escaped before it is shown. The API’s CORS setting and Cognito’s callback URLs accept only the CloudFront domain and http://localhost:5500 for local testing. Protecting the API and the Account Throttling: each route accepts 10 requests per second, with bursts of 20. Extra requests get 429 at the gateway, so a flood cannot use up all 10 concurrent Lambdas that a new account has. The replayer retries 429 safely, because the same payload produces the same eventId. Input validation: tracking codes, query parameters, and payload shapes are all checked, and bad input returns 400. Least privilege: every Lambda role gets only the actions it needs on this stack’s resources. Permissions boundary: every role in the stack carries the boundary shipment-sla-boundary. The deploy role may create or change a role only if that boundary is attached, and it is explicitly denied removing or editing the boundary. Even a stolen deploy token could not create an administrator role. No long-lived keys: GitHub Actions gets a temporary role through OIDC. The role trusts only this repository, matched by GitHub’s fixed numeric owner and repository IDs, and only the approved production environment. 📷 Screenshots to add: the response headers in the browser developer tools, and the web bucket’s “Block all public access” setting.

title: Orchestration, Security, and Monitoring
content:
Orchestration, Security, and Monitoring The Workflow EventBridge starts the state machine every day at 18:00 UTC, which is 01:00 the next morning in Vietnam. The Step Functions states, in order:
InitializeRun fixes one run ID and one UTC date. Every stage receives both. AcquireLock writes the lock item to DynamoDB only if no lock exists. If one already exists, the run ends at PipelineBusy without touching any data. Ingest, BronzeToSilver, and SilverToGold each start a Glue job and wait for it to finish. ReadGoldVersions reads the record the Gold job wrote, and GoldVersionsValid checks that it belongs to this run and names all three tables. BuildCompletion and PublishCompletion write state/pipeline/latest.json with the three Iceberg snapshot IDs. ReleaseLock deletes the lock, but only if this execution still owns it. If any step fails, the workflow goes to ReleaseFailedLock and ends as failed. The whole run has a 90-minute limit, and each Glue job has its own timeout and allows only one run at a time.
📷 Screenshot to add: a successful execution graph in Step Functions.
When a Run Is Killed A timeout or a manual abort skips ReleaseLock, so the lock would stay and block the next night’s run. The lock-janitor Lambda handles this case. It runs when an execution ends as FAILED, TIMED_OUT, or ABORTED, and again every 15 minutes. It deletes the lock only when:
the execution that owns the lock has ended, and none of the three Glue jobs is still running. The delete is conditional on the owner it just inspected. The janitor never starts or stops anything. Its decision (released, waiting_for_glue, owner_running, or no_lock) is written to its log.
Security Every stage has its own IAM role: ingestion, Silver, Gold, Step Functions, EventBridge, the health monitor, the janitor, and the dashboard reader. Each role can touch only the S3 prefixes it needs. Runtime roles can read their scripts but cannot change them. Only Step Functions can write the completion marker. The dashboard role can read published data, run Athena queries, and write its own query results. It cannot change the lake or start a job. All three buckets are private, encrypted, and reject plain HTTP. The lake and script buckets keep versions for 30 days. No access key is stored anywhere. AWS services use their roles, and I use short-lived credentials. scripts/check_permissions.py runs IAM policy simulations against the deployed roles (69 of 69 passed on the last check). Checkov scans the Terraform code on every pull request, and every accepted finding has a written reason next to the resource. Monitoring The health-monitor Lambda runs every 15 minutes and reads only metadata: the completion marker, the Silver pointer, and the manifest. It sends two metrics to CloudWatch:
Healthy: 1 when the run IDs match, ingestion succeeded, and the data is under 26 hours old. SourceSuccessRatio: the share of boards that answered successfully. Six alarms send email through SNS:
Alarm Fires when pipeline-failed an execution fails pipeline-timed-out an execution hits the 90-minute limit pipeline-aborted an execution is stopped pipeline-unhealthy Healthy is below 1, or missing, for two 15-minute periods source-coverage-low fewer than 100% of boards succeed for two periods lock-janitor-errors the janitor Lambda itself throws an error A missing Healthy metric counts as unhealthy. So if the monitor itself stops running, that is noticed too.
Logs are kept for 30 days for Glue and 14 days for Lambda. They live in CloudWatch Logs, under one log group per job and per function.
📷 Screenshots to add: the CloudWatch alarm list and the SNS alert email.

title: Workshop
content:
Workshop: OnTime Radar This workshop shows how I built OnTime Radar, a serverless AWS service that tracks shipments across several carriers and warns staff when deliveries start running late. It has been running on my AWS account since 16 November 2026, fed every 15 minutes with real historical orders from the public Olist dataset.
Why this project A shop that ships through several carriers has the same few problems every day. Each carrier reports status in its own format. Updates arrive twice or out of order. Customer service has to check several websites to answer one question. And late deliveries are discovered only when a customer complains. OnTime Radar gathers every carrier’s events into one reliable timeline per shipment, measures on-time performance by carrier and region, and sends an email alert when the late rate climbs.
What you will build A webhook API that accepts three carrier formats and keeps each shipment’s events in order. A DynamoDB timeline that ignores duplicates and refuses impossible status changes. An S3 event lake with SLA reports in Athena. A web dashboard on CloudFront with Cognito login and two staff roles. CloudWatch alarms with email alerts, a daily health check, and a chaos test. Automatic deployment from GitHub Actions through OIDC, with no stored access keys. Who this is for Readers who know the basics of Lambda, IAM, and S3 and want to see an event-driven system that handles messy real-world input. You need an AWS account, the AWS SAM CLI, and .NET 10. Section 5.1.2 lists the exact tools.

title: Dashboard, Testing, and Results
content:
Dashboard, Testing, and Results What the Dashboard Checks Before Showing Anything The Streamlit app always switches to the read-only dashboard role first. Then it:
Makes sure no pipeline run currently holds the lock. Reads the completion marker, the Silver pointer, and the matching manifest. Checks that all three agree on the run ID and UTC date, that ingestion succeeded, and that the data is less than 26 hours old. Queries fact_job_posting with FOR VERSION AS OF the snapshot ID named in the marker. Repeats steps 1–3 after the query. If anything changed in between, it throws the result away and shows a message instead. It never falls back to “the newest date in the table”. Stale or half-published data is refused, not displayed.
What the Dashboard Shows Filters for platform, role family, location, and work mode, plus a search on title or company. Number of postings, companies, and locations, and the remote share. Postings by role family, and the top employers. A table of postings with links to the original job page. Publication time, data age, board coverage, the Athena query ID, and the bytes scanned. Overview of the published snapshot of 21 November 2026.
Postings table with links to the original job pages.
Opening It Locally $env:AWS_REGION = 'ap-southeast-1' $env:LAKE_BUCKET = terraform -chdir=infra output -raw lake_bucket $env:PIPELINE_LOCK_TABLE = terraform -chdir=infra output -raw pipeline_lock_table $env:ATHENA_DATABASE = terraform -chdir=infra output -raw gold_database $env:ATHENA_WORKGROUP = terraform -chdir=infra output -raw athena_workgroup $env:AWS_DASHBOARD_ROLE_ARN = terraform -chdir=infra output -raw dashboard_reader_role_arn .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m streamlit run dashboard/app.py --server.address 127.0.0.1 Then open http://localhost:8501 and press Refresh data. Viewing data does not deploy anything or start a run.
Automated Tests Every pull request runs ruff, 251 pytest tests, terraform validate, and a Checkov scan in GitHub Actions. The tests mock the job APIs and AWS, and cover:
ingestion: retries, failed and empty boards, page limits, parallel fetching order, manifest commit order; Silver: identity, deduplication, every lifecycle case in 5.2.4, and Data Quality preparation; Gold: the three marts, role families, empty-day overwrite, and Iceberg writes; the dashboard and both Lambdas: locks, stale or changed publication, and janitor decisions; the repository itself: evidence files are valid JSON and contain no AWS account ID. Testing Failure Cases on AWS Scenario How to trigger it Expected result A second run while one is active Start a manual execution during the nightly run It ends at PipelineBusy, and no data changes A board stops answering Happened for real with Lever mistral in November source-coverage-low goes to ALARM; Silver keeps the board’s postings as unverified Data becomes stale Pause the schedule for more than 26 hours pipeline-unhealthy fires, and the dashboard refuses to show data A run is aborted Stop an execution in the console pipeline-aborted fires; the janitor releases the lock once Glue is idle (Fill in: the date you ran each scenario, plus a screenshot or log line as proof.)
Measured Results These are dated observations, not a live status:
Measurement Value Scheduled runs that succeeded, 15 Sep – 21 Nov 2026 68 of 68 Open postings on 21 Nov 2026 8,672 from 467 employers Boards collected on 21 Nov 2026 36 of 36 Time from trigger to published Gold (median, 14–20 Nov) 9 minutes Glue cost per run (before credits) about USD 0.11 Bytes scanned by one dashboard query about 1 MiB The run-time and cost figures were measured with scripts/run_metrics.py before parallel fetching and Iceberg were added. That change also removed the crawler, so the cost per run is now lower. Gold can hold more rows than one run’s Bronze, because postings from a board that failed keep their last observation while they are still fresh.

title: Monitoring and Testing
content:
Monitoring and Testing Alarms Alarm Fires when Why it is built this way LateDeliveryAlarm late deliveries are 20% or more of deliveries in 2 of 3 consecutive 15-minute windows, counting only windows with at least 10 deliveries The first version fired on “5 late per hour” and flipped three times in one morning as traffic grew (see 5.1.8). A rate that must last is quieter and still catches real problems DlqAlarm the dead-letter queue holds at least one message A message that failed five times needs a person to look at it Both alarms email through SNS, once when they go to ALARM and once when they return to OK. The late-delivery email links to the “needs attention” page. The trade-off is that a real problem is reported after about 30–45 minutes instead of at once.
All Lambda logs are kept in CloudWatch Logs for 14 days.
📷 Screenshots to add: the two alarms in CloudWatch, and an alarm email (hide the address).
Daily Check One read-only command checks the whole system in about 40 seconds:
.\tools\daily-check.ps1 -SaveTo docs\evidence Result on 23 November 2026 at 18:16:
# Check Result 1 CloudFormation stack UPDATE_COMPLETE 2 Replayer schedule ENABLED 3 Replayer in the last hour 4 runs, 404 events sent, 0 failed; 13,580 of 98,202 orders replayed 4 Lambda in the last 24 hours 0 errors, 0 throttles 5 SQS and DLQ 0 waiting, DLQ 0 6 Event lake today 688 files in events/dt=2026-11-23/ 7 CloudWatch alarms both OK 8 API /health 200, report without token 401 9 Website HTTP 200, 4 of 4 security headers 10 Alert email 1 confirmed subscription All 11 lines passed.
Automated Tests dotnet test runs more than 200 tests (212 were recorded on 23 November) without AWS or Docker:
Core: the status rules, the three adapters, and the simulator. Service: the real API, processor, and store code, running against small in-memory fakes of DynamoDB, SQS, S3, and Athena. A fake throws an error for any call it does not understand, so a code change cannot silently bypass it. To prove the tests catch real mistakes, I broke the code on purpose in three risky places and checked that the tests failed (mutation testing):
Area Deliberate bug Result Store treat any failed condition as a duplicate test fails Processor ignore the FIFO rule after a failure in a batch 2 tests fail Authorization remove the role check from /sla/trend 2 tests fail GitHub Actions runs the build, the tests, and sam validate --lint on every push.

Item Value Shipments / distinct events 87 / 480 Webhooks sent 2,375: each event about 5 times, shuffled within each shipment, plus 24 broken payloads Accepted (202) / rejected (400) 2,351 / 24, exactly as expected History items in DynamoDB 480, one per event Differences from the answer key 0 DLQ before → after 0 → 0 Time from receive to processed, p50 / p95 / max 17 / 40 / 192 ms The test data used DEMO tracking codes, so it does not affect the SLA reports.

title: Cost and Cleanup
content:
Cost and Cleanup Cost Estimate This section is in progress. The figure below is an early estimate. The final report needs the measured cost from Cost Explorer and a saved AWS Pricing Calculator estimate based on that traffic.
With the replayer running every 15 minutes (about 1,900 orders and 9,000 events a day), I estimate about USD 3–5 per month. DynamoDB writes are the largest item, because every event writes a status item and a history item in one transaction.
Service What drives the cost Note DynamoDB (on-demand) writes per event, plus queries from the dashboard largest item Lambda (arm64) API, processor, and replayer invocations mostly within the free tier API Gateway (HTTP API) webhook and dashboard requests SQS FIFO messages and retries S3 event lake, dataset, website small amounts of data Athena bytes scanned capped at 1 GB per query, and most queries are served from cache CloudFront, Cognito, CloudWatch, SNS traffic, users, logs, alarms, emails low use (To fill in: the Cost Explorer figures per service for a full week, and a link to the saved Pricing Calculator estimate.)
📷 Screenshot to add: Cost Explorer filtered to this project’s services, grouped by service.
How the Design Keeps Cost Down No servers and no VPC: Lambda and managed services only, so there is no NAT gateway, which would cost more than the whole application. arm64 (Graviton) Lambdas: about 20% cheaper than x86 for the same running time. DynamoDB on-demand: pay per request, with nothing to pay while the system is idle. Athena limits: a 1 GB cap per query, partition projection so only the requested days are scanned, and a two-layer cache that served 79% of report queries without a scan. Throttling at API Gateway, so a flood of requests is rejected before it runs Lambda. 14-day log retention instead of keeping logs forever. Cleanup Delete the resources only after the project has been graded. Follow this order:
Stop the replay: set ReplayState to DISABLED and deploy, or disable the schedule in EventBridge Scheduler.
Save any evidence you need: the daily-check files, screenshots, and Cost Explorer exports.
Empty the two buckets. CloudFormation cannot delete a bucket that still contains objects.
aws s3 rm "s3://<DataBucketName>" --recursive aws s3 rm "s3://<web bucket>" --recursive Delete the application stack:
sam delete --stack-name shipment-sla This removes the API, Lambdas, queues, table, Cognito user pool, CloudFront distribution, alarms, Glue table, and Athena workgroup.
Delete the deployment stack github-oidc-deploy (the OIDC provider, the deploy role, and the boundary):
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name github-oidc-deploy --region ap-southeast-1 In GitHub, remove the AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN secret and the production environment.
Check that nothing is left: in the console, look at CloudFormation, S3, CloudFront, and CloudWatch log groups in ap-southeast-1. Then check the bill a day later.

title: Cost, Cleanup, and Reflection
content:
Cost, Cleanup, Limitations, and Reflection Cost Controls The project uses daily batch processing, serverless query, small Glue worker settings, stage timeouts, retention rules, Athena scan limits, and a monthly budget alert.
Measured Cost scripts/run_metrics.py measured the 7 scheduled runs of 14–20 November 2026 and compared them with Cost Explorer. These are list prices before credits:
Item Per run (median) Glue jobs (3 jobs, 517 DPU-seconds) USD 0.064 (Cost Explorer: USD 0.0635) Glue crawler USD 0.049 Glue total about USD 0.11 Lambda, Step Functions, EventBridge, 6 alarms within the free tier S3, DynamoDB a few cents per day With one run per day, that is about USD 3.4 per month for Glue. These runs were measured before parallel fetching and Iceberg were added. That change removed the crawler, which was about 44% of the Glue cost per run, so the current cost should be closer to USD 2 per month. This lower figure is an estimate until a full week is measured again.
(To fill in: a link to the saved AWS Pricing Calculator estimate based on these numbers.)
Budget alerts notify; they do not stop spending.
Storage Retention Data Default retention Bronze and ingestion manifests 30 days Quality results 90 days Athena query results 7 days Glue temporary data 7 days Silver, Gold, and state No automatic expiration Versioned noncurrent objects can remain billable after current-object expiration.
Safe Cleanup Disable the EventBridge pipeline schedule. Confirm that no Step Functions execution, Glue job, or crawler is running. Confirm the DynamoDB lock state and follow the recovery runbook if a run was interrupted. Export any evidence that must be retained. Review terraform plan -destroy. Use the explicit bucket cleanup option only after confirming that retained project data may be deleted. Run terraform destroy. Verify that subscriptions, alarms, log groups, buckets, and scheduled rules are removed as intended. Destroying the stack can remove retained data. Cleanup must never be performed without reviewing exact targets and required evidence.
Known Limitations Arbeitnow pagination is capped at two pages. Gold publication is not atomic across all three marts. Role classification uses title rules and can overlap. Missing remote metadata does not prove that a posting is onsite. The configured sources do not represent the complete labor market. The local dashboard is not a public multi-user application. Historical results are not proof of current pipeline health. Personal Reflection The project helped me connect individual AWS services into an operational data system. The most important learning was that successful data processing is not enough: the system must preserve observation identity, distinguish source failure from business change, enforce quality before publication, restrict permissions, expose health signals, and give consumers a way to reject stale results.
AI support accelerated research, implementation, review, and documentation, but it also made validation more important. I needed to inspect proposed code, compare it with AWS service behavior, run tests, review permissions, and verify results instead of accepting generated output without evidence.
Items Remaining for Final Submission Screenshots for the main deployment and validation steps (the architecture diagram and dashboard screenshots are done). Saved AWS Pricing Calculator estimate. Confirmed personal troubleshooting examples and contribution details. Final review of image captions and bilingual terminology.

title: Troubleshooting and Future Work
content:
Troubleshooting and Future Work These problems came up while building and running OnTime Radar. Each one lists the commit that fixed it in the ontime-radar repository.
Problems I Hit 1. The API started answering 503 once real traffic arrived Symptom: with the Olist replay running, API Gateway answered some webhooks with 503. Cause: a new AWS account can run only 10 Lambdas at the same time. The FIFO processor scaled to one instance per shipment group and took all 10, leaving nothing for the API. Fix: I limited the processor’s SQS trigger to 2 concurrent instances. Asking AWS for a higher quota is the next step. Commit: e835dd5 (16/11). 2. A secret file was almost committed Symptom: samconfig.toml, which holds the webhook secret, showed up as an untracked file even though it was listed in .gitignore. Cause: the line had a comment after the pattern. In .gitignore, text after the pattern on the same line becomes part of the pattern, so it never matched. Fix: I moved the comment to its own line. Commit: d77358c (16/11). 3. The late-delivery alarm kept flipping Symptom: the first alarm fired at “5 or more late deliveries per hour”. With about 80 deliveries an hour, it went into ALARM three times in one morning. Cause: a fixed count grows with traffic, so a busier hour looks like an incident. Fix: the alarm now uses the late rate: 20% or more in 2 of 3 windows, counting only windows with at least 10 deliveries. It also sends an “all clear” email. Commit: b6c2dfa (19/11). 4. GitHub could not assume the deploy role Symptom: the first OIDC deployment was denied at AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Cause: GitHub’s token now carries the owner and repository IDs in its sub claim (repo:owner@<id>/repo@<id>:...). The trust policy expected names only. Fix: the trust policy matches the fixed IDs. This is also safer: a new repository created with the same name cannot use the role. Commit: 01b4e9c (20/11). 5. The replayer could skip failed orders Symptom: when a few webhooks in a run failed, the cursor still moved forward, so those orders were never sent again. Fix: responses are now sorted into Sent, Rejected (bad data that resending cannot fix), and Failed (throttling, 5xx, network). The cursor moves only when Failed is 0. Resending is safe because duplicates are dropped. Commit: 81576a1 (20/11). 6. Broken payloads returned 500 instead of 400 Symptom: the chaos generator found that a body that is not a JSON object, or a number sent as a string, made the adapters throw. The API returned 500, and a real carrier would keep retrying a 500 forever. Fix: every adapter now checks the JSON shape and value types first and returns 400. I added 7 regression tests. Commit: ac243b0 (23/11). 7. Other problems (to be filled in) (Add problems that are not in the commit history, for example console errors or AccessDenied messages during the first deployment, with the same layout: symptom, cause, fix.)
Known Limitations Limitation Effect today Possible fix R1: two events with exactly the same timestamp; the one that arrives later wins 0 shipments affected: the replay data never has equal timestamps Break ties with a fixed order (status rank, then source code) R2: a promised date sent only on an event that arrives late is lost, so the shipment is not counted in the on-time rate 0 shipments affected: the replayer sends the promised date on every webhook Let a Stale event fill empty fields without changing the status DynamoDB and S3 are not written in one transaction If the Lambda stops between the two writes, the event is missing from Athena. Lookups and alarms are not affected Write the lake from DynamoDB Streams Lateness compares the UTC date with the promised date 280 of 96,470 orders (0.29 percentage points) are counted late although they arrived in the evening of the promised day in Brazil Compare in the delivery region’s time zone Carriers, tracking codes, and in-transit steps are simulated Failed-attempt rates do not reflect real carriers Connect real carrier APIs The data is from Brazil Regions are Brazilian states, not Vietnamese provinces Use Vietnamese order data when available Each R1/R2 gap has a test named Known_gap_... that records today’s behaviour, so fixing the rule forces the test to change too.

Give each carrier its own secret, or sign webhooks with HMAC, stored in Secrets Manager. Narrow the S3 permissions of the processor and the replayer. Add a lifecycle rule for Athena results, and stop a query that times out. Write the event lake from DynamoDB Streams, to close the gap described above. title: Troubleshooting and Future Work
content:
Troubleshooting and Future Work This page records problems I actually ran into while building and running the pipeline, what caused them, and how I fixed them. Each entry points to the commit where the fix landed, so the story can be checked against the repository.
Problems I Hit 1. One job board stopped returning data Symptom: from 6 November the source-coverage-low alarm stayed in ALARM, and Mistral AI postings stopped updating. Cause: the company moved its careers page from Lever to Ashby. The old Lever board answered with HTTP 404, so the ingestion job counted it as a failed board every day. Fix: I replaced the Lever entry with the Ashby board mistral.ai in ingestion/sources.json, which kept the catalog at 36 boards. I also added a test that rejects a company listed under two platforms, because that would count its postings twice. Lesson: a coverage alarm is only useful if someone reads it. This one fired for two weeks before I acted on it. Commit: be0e63f (21/11/2026). 📷 Add: the CloudWatch alarm history showing ALARM, then OK after the fix.
2. The next day’s run refused to start (PipelineBusy) Symptom: the 01:00 run stopped immediately with PipelineBusy. Cause: a previous execution had timed out. A timeout skips the ReleaseLock step, so the DynamoDB lock stayed in the table, and every later run saw it and backed off. Fix: I added a small Lambda (“lock janitor”). It runs when an execution ends as FAILED, TIMED_OUT, or ABORTED, and again every 15 minutes. It deletes the lock only when the owning execution has finished and no Glue job or crawler is still running, and the delete is conditional on the owner it inspected. Verification: terraform apply added 11 resources, and a real invoke returned no_lock. Commit: 9dacb34 (21/11/2026). 3. Re-running a day could leave old rows in Gold Symptom: a test showed that re-running a day whose mart came out empty still left the previous rows in the table. Cause: Spark’s dynamic partition overwrite only replaces partitions that receive new rows. An empty result touches no partition, so nothing is replaced. Fix: the Gold job overwrites the requested snapshot_date explicitly, in a single Iceberg commit. Commit: d733030 (22/11/2026). 4. Iceberg and Parquet tables “did not match” Symptom: after the first Iceberg shadow write, both copies had the same row counts (8,682 / 15 / 15), but an EXCEPT comparison reported every row as different. Cause: Athena reads Parquet timestamps at millisecond precision, while Iceberg keeps Spark’s microseconds. The values were the same moment written with different precision. Fix: the comparison script rounds timestamps to milliseconds before comparing. Day 1 then showed 0 differing rows in both directions. Commit: 7ab87d9 (23/11/2026). 5. Parallel fetching could run out of memory Symptom (found during design, before it failed in production): a single run produces about 150 MB of Bronze JSON, while Glue Python Shell has about 1 GB of RAM. Cause: fetching all 36 boards in parallel and only writing at the end would hold every response in memory at once. Fix: 5 worker threads fetch the boards. Results are written to S3 one at a time, in board order, and at most 10 boards are held in memory. A failed S3 write still aborts the whole run. Commit: 066c331 (22/11/2026). 6. A lint upgrade would have broken the Glue job Symptom: after adding ruff, its upgrade rules wanted to rewrite code to use datetime.UTC. Cause: datetime.UTC only exists from Python 3.11, but Glue Python Shell runs Python 3.9. Fix: I set target-version = "py39" in pyproject.toml so the linter only suggests syntax the runtime supports. Commit: 37d537f (21/11/2026). 7. Smaller fixes Problem Fix Commit A unit test failed because Spark guessed the Bronze schema differently from production Declared the schema explicitly in the test fixture d1136a4 (28/07) The dashboard broke after a Streamlit upgrade removed use_container_width Switched to width="stretch" a9dd23e (29/07) Vietnamese text in the docs turned into broken characters Forced UTF-8 and added a test that checks file encoding e829916 (20/11) CI failed because pandas was missing Added it to requirements-dev.txt 44cf03d (20/11) 8. Other problems (to be filled in) (Add any problem that never made it into a commit, for example console errors, IAM AccessDenied messages, or a failed terraform apply, using the same layout: symptom, cause, fix, and how you checked.)
Future Work (Draft list. Keep the items you actually plan, and remove the rest.)
Switch readers to Iceberg. Athena and the dashboard still read the Parquet copy. Once the shadow comparison stays clean for several days, they can read Iceberg, and the three marts can then be published together. Lift the Arbeitnow page limit. The feed is capped at two pages, so some postings are skipped. A shared dashboard. The Streamlit app runs only on my machine. A hosted, read-only version would let other people use it without AWS credentials. Deploy from CI. CI already runs tests, terraform validate, and Checkov. The next step is a reviewed plan on each pull request, using short-lived OIDC credentials. Better role classification. Titles are mapped to roles with rules. A labelled sample would show how often those rules are wrong.
